[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives BOTH roots \(\dfrac{17 \pm \sqrt{33}}{2}\). Squaring \(\sqrt{x} = 8 - x\) introduces an extraneous root: the equation requires \(8 - x \ge 0\), and at \(x = \dfrac{17 + \sqrt{33}}{2} \approx 11.372\) the left side is \(+0.372\) while the right is \(-6.372\). Only \(x = \dfrac{17 - \sqrt{33}}{2} \approx 5.628\) satisfies the original equation, where both sides equal \(-0.628\).]

[Textbook misprint: the item is printed \(\log_{1/2}(-8) = 3\), which is false twice over — the argument is negative, and \(\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{8}\). The book's key answers \(8 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{-3}\), i.e. it reads the question as \(\log_{1/2} 8 = -3\): the minus sign was typeset onto the \(8\) instead of the \(3\). The intended question is solved above.]
[Textbook misprint (notation only): the printed key writes the range as \([0, \infty]\), with a closed bracket at infinity. Infinity is not attained, so the range is \([0, \infty)\).]

[Textbook error, answer-affecting: the printed solution states "From graph when \(x = 3\), \(y = -5\) so \(g(3) = -5\)", but that disagrees with the book's OWN figure. On Fig. 6.14 the curve's minimum marker sits at the same height on the page as the labelled point \((-6, -4)\) — two points at the same height have the same \(y\)-value — so the minimum is at \(y \approx -4\), and \(g(3) \approx -4\), a full unit above the printed value. The companion reading \(g(-4) = 0\) is confirmed correct by the figure.]

[Textbook error, answer-affecting: at the "Using Power rule" step the book turns \(\left[\log 2 + \log (x-4)^{2}\right]\) into \(\left[\log 2 - 2\log (x-4)\right]\) — the inner sign flips from \(+\) to \(-\) for no reason — and carries the error into its final line. The correct expansion is \(3\log x + \log(x+3) - \log 2 - 2\log(x-4)\).]

[Textbook error, answer-affecting: the printed solution correctly reaches \(|x| > 4\) and then states the COMPLEMENT of it, \(-4 < x < 4\), i.e. \(x \in (-4, 4)\). The correct domain is \((-\infty, -4) \cup (4, \infty)\). On the printed answer the function is undefined everywhere in the stated interval — at \(x = 0\), \(\bigl||0| - 1\bigr| - 3 = -2 < 0\).]

[Textbook error, answer-affecting: having found \([x] \in \{1, 2\}\) the book never substitutes back into its own equation \(3\{x\} = 2[x] - 2\); it simply unions the two intervals and prints \(x \in [1, 3)\). Substituting gives \(\{x\} = 0\) for \([x] = 1\) and \(\{x\} = \dfrac{2}{3}\) for \([x] = 2\), so the solution set is the two points \(\left\{1, \dfrac{8}{3}\right\}\). Counterexample against the printed interval: at \(x = 1.5\) the left side is \(3(0.5) = 1.5\) and the right side is \(2(1) - 2 = 0\).]

[Textbook defect: this is a multiple-correct item reused as a single-answer MCQ. The equation's roots are \(x = 4\) and \(x = 2^{-1/3}\), and both are admissible, so ALL FOUR printed statements are true at once — one root is irrational, neither is prime, both are real, and one is an integer. Option C is retained because it characterises the whole solution set, but any of the other three is equally defensible as printed.]

[Textbook misprint (labelling only): the four alternatives are printed A), B), C), C) — the fourth option carries the label C) instead of D). It is stored here as D so the row carries a valid A-D set; the option texts are verbatim.]

[Textbook misprint (punctuation only): options B and D separate their two entries with a FULL STOP rather than a comma, printed \(\{-2.\,2\}\) and \((-2.\,2)\). Other questions on the same page use clear commas. The intended set and interval are \(\{-2, 2\}\) and \((-2, 2)\); note these are a SET and an INTERVAL and are therefore genuinely different answers, not duplicates. The stem also misspells "equal" as "euqal".]

[Textbook misprint (typesetting only): the composite is printed with mismatched brackets, opening with \((\) and closing with \(]\). The intended triple composite is unambiguous, and the answer is the same under every bracketing since the function has order 3.]

[Textbook omission: the printed answer key for this Miscellaneous exercise stops PART-WAY THROUGH Q39 — its last two sub-items, (g) and (h), are unanswered — while the exercise itself continues to Q44. Q40 to Q44 all have determinate answers (Q40 asks for domains in seven parts, Q41 for ranges in five), so this is not the usual pattern of a key skipping proofs: twenty-one answerable parts are simply unanswered. Every answer from Q39(g) onward was derived directly and checked by substitution, with no key to compare against.]

[Textbook misprint (labelling): this question's sub-items are printed a), c), c), d), e), f), g), h) — there is no b), and two consecutive items are both labelled c). The first of the two is stored here as (b), which also matches the book's own key, whose b) entry is \(\{-2, 2, 4\}\).]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \((-2, 8)\). Since \([x]\) is an integer, \(-2 < [x]\) forces \([x] \ge -1\) and hence \(x \ge -1\), so the solution set is \([-1, 8)\). The key's interval wrongly admits every \(x\) in \((-2, -1)\): at \(x = -1.5\), \([x] = -2\) and \(-2 < -2\) is false.]

[Textbook omission: the printed key for this question answers sub-items a), b), c), d), f), g), h), i) and j) but omits (e). The answer given here is derived without a key to check against.]

[Textbook misprint (label only, value correct): the key prints this answer as "gog", but \(9x^2 - 12x + 4 = (3x-2)^2\) is \(g(f(x))\), i.e. gof. A genuine \(g\circ g\) would be \(x^4\), and the question asks for fog and gof, not gog.]

[Textbook misprint: the stem excludes \(x \ne \dfrac{5}{2}\), but the denominator \(5x - 2\) vanishes at \(x = \dfrac{2}{5}\) — the digits are transposed. The identity asked for holds throughout the domain either way, so the result is unaffected.]
